description:
Unlike its successor aesthetic Funfair Kitsch , which emerged from the post-war industrialization of the amusement sector and prioritizes mass-produced and airbrushed visual maximalism inspired by contemporary pop culture, Fairground Baroque is characterized by the slow application of hand-carved woodwork, neoclassical sculptures, polychrome painting, and gold leaf ornamentation to create a specifically theatrical form of public architecture.

The term "baroque" is used here descriptively rather than as a strict art historical category. Fairground artisans drew freely from baroque , rococo , neoclassical , romantic , and symbolist traditions, transposing and mixing these styles to produce a uniquely playful and extravagant visual aesthetic tailored to the demands of the travelling fair: lightweight, modular, and visually overwhelming enough to command attention in an open public square.
culturalContext: Key values (per the Aesthetics Wiki): Craftsmanship, spectacle, wonder, transience, community, artisan tradition
